author: swatcoder
text: Is it forcing us to "pay off" technical debt or is it starting us on a compulsory endless treadmill of feature-neutral fix-work? Collectively, we just won't know for a while. It totally feels like the former if you watch it find and fix vulnerabilities or other debt-tasks one after another. But only so many of these "technical debt" issue are little off-by-one errors that get remedied by a surgically narrow patch. Many enough require some kind of restructuring or redevelopment of their own and it's going to take time to figure out if AI faces the same dilemma as human developers: where each non-trivial change carries the risk of some new issue, ad infinitum. If that happens to be the case, and AI isn't able to magically produce perfect software in finite time, then what's really happened is that the threat of hostile AI exploiting our technical debt will force us to always be burning and churning code just to remain a moving target. It's another "we'll see" thing for now, I think.

author: sleepyams
text: I honestly think there are some kind of laws of physics at play here... in the statistical limit of the massively participatory interaction of engineers, there is some kind of least action principle where the system is seeking lower energy (i.e. less code complexity, better foundations, etc), but only locally.  The path towards a radically better foundation for the entire industry is outside of the "energy well" that it is currently in---at least that's how I see it.  I feel like that's why we see more things like elegant scripting languages rather than ground-up reimaginings of computing itself. There is a concept of the hourglass model [0] of internet protocols, where IP sits at the waist.  I believe that similar things are probably true in any "stack" based structure, such as computing, where the protocol at the waist has the most staying power (which at the current moment could be e.g. x86, or something) because it's essentially the universal translation layer that enables all the language protocols built above it to be agnostic to all the transport protocols below it.  So, I see it as an open question as to what the best way to affect change in a situation like this is.  I'm interested in if anyone else has any thoughts along these lines. [0] https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hourglass_model

author: jmyeet
text: I think we'll look back at this moment as peak C/C++ before they begin a long, slow decline into irrelevance. I've been bullish on Rust for years because memory safety is simply too important and Rust can essentially prove an implementation correct and solve a certain class of very important bugs. It doesn't solve every problem and there is a complexity cost. I've also said that writing multithreaded code is simply too complex. In an era of out-of-order execution, different levels of caching, asymmetric cores, hyperthreading (although this is largely dead now?), branch prediction and having to support multiple architectures it's simply too hard for most people to write correct multithreaded code. Period. If you find yourself as a non-library developer creating a mutex or spawning a thread, somebody has screwed up. This is also why I think the single-threaded async/await model with post-request teardown of PHP is the correct choice for most people. We're going to go through a dark period of a lot of 0days. As the article notes, this is paying 40 years of technical debt. It will result in a more secure ecosystem however. I believe this will ultimately also hamper black markets, governments and 3 letter agencies who trade in those 0days. As painful as this all is, it will ultimately be a good thing, one of the few to come out of AI (IMHO).

author: mpyne
text: OK, I think I see what’s going on with this, in this configuration. The goal from an attacker’s perspective is to get this to be true: `$ret = crypt($pw, $hash); $ret == $hash` when called by OpenSSH’s sshd. This is how sshd validates that the user logging in knew the account password. The `$hash` is the “settings” to the crypt call and will normally look like “$6$--gibberish” for users with passwords set, but could look like “*” or “!” for users not intended to be able to login. The bug is from the intersection of all of these things: 1. musl can return “*” for errors, rather than leave the return value NULL. Other libc have adopted something like this too, but seem to use a different result “*0”. 2. musl can also return “+” for errors, but only does so if $hash starts with “*”. This is intended to eliminate the possibility of an error causing `$ret == $hash` to be true, however it assumes that applications calling `crypt()` will set $pw and $hash to values corresponding to the `$ret == $hash` comparison to be made immediately afterwards. 3. OpenSSH can be convinced to pass the hash of a different user if the hash is “*” or “!” to avoid timing attacks that can enumerate the user list, so it will set $pw and $hash to correspond to different users. $hash will be a real “$6$--gibberish” style hash in this case, and OpenSSH expects `crypt()` to either return NULL or return a hash string. But now there’s two hashes OpenSSH uses. It does: `$ret = crypt($pw, $hash2); $ret == $hash1`; 4. This should normally not be a problem because OpenSSH will pass in valid $pw and $hash2 that should not lead to errors in hashing, so the $ret that musl generates should be a real hash that cannot match the “*” or “!” $hash1 for the login-disabled user. However as a DDoS mitigation, musl will return error if the password is too long when using SHA-2-based hashes (the default, it seems). 5. This error will result in a non-NULL result of “*” or “+”. Since OpenSSH passed in a real hash ($hash2), musl will return “*”, which compares equal to the actual user hash $hash1 for the disabled-login user. The OpenSSL adjustment ensures a minimum hash length for the user before logging them in, even if crypt() succeeds somehow.

author: amluto
text: The whole story is a bit worse than this.  Musl already worked around this type of failure .  See the second-to-last line here: https://git.musl-libc.org/cgit/musl/tree/src/crypt/crypt_des... (hey, this workaround is wrong if the salt is "x"!) but they forgot to work around it here: https://git.musl-libc.org/cgit/musl/tree/src/crypt/crypt_sha... The vulnerable path in musl is only a little bit vulnerable, because "*" is not actually a sha256 encrypted configuration and should not reach this code: musl's crypt(..., "*") will not call that code!  Turns out that sshd detects that the password hash is too short and does not forward the salt ! https://github.com/openssh/openssh-portable/blob/master/auth... Look, no else statement!  If that if doesn't get taken, then salt remains NULL.  And the sshd code is really quite messy and doesn't keep track of the fact that this code path is inappropriate for validating an existing password hash. A workaround in the sha256 path in musl wouldn't even have prevented the bug! I'm going to give some credit to musl for unwisely using "*" and some credit to OpenSSH for having nonsensical control and data flow.

author: aljgz
text: My general rule of thumb is: "no magic strings". This is much easier to implement in higher-level languages and when writing application/web code than system programming. Don't return empty string/asterisk/anything else. Instead, return a failure value. When absolutely needed, choose the magic string with more caution: One string showing the SHA-256 of a non-existing hash? It's a good idea for it to be a valid hash. Now we have a new risk: if it's broken once, it's broken for all. So it's a good idea for it to be a random one for each machine and/or account. Even this might have problems I can't think of, but it seems to be as secure as an account with a real password. If this is not a good decision for some reason, choose something unmistakable: "--ACCOUNT-HAS-NO-PASSWORD--". This is much less likely to be mistakenly used in a different context, is much easier to look up in a code base than "*", and is self-documenting.

author: wolrah
text: Also how many times do we have to learn that letting badly programmed software die when unexpected things happen is the better option because it means people actually notice that there's a problem.  Silent compatibility hacks are the worst, they guarantee problems never get fixed and the stack of hacks never gets smaller. Microsoft has historically been one of the leaders on the wrong side of this one, but they have also demonstrated how effective it is to call out badly behaved software and make it annoy the users with UAC.  When Vista came out, so many applications needed elevated privileges to run because they were badly designed to write user data in system locations, but now their application was more annoying to use and came with a scary dialog about it making changes to your computer that other better-designed software didn't get. More often than not if a program didn't actually intend to change system settings it was just a matter of badly chosen default paths which are pretty trivial to fix, but so many vendors just would not do it despite years of complaints from NT admins wanting to not have to spend hours with Process Explorer figuring out specific permissions to grant limited users enough access.  Once their failures were put front and center, calling their application out as the one getting things wrong every time the user ran it, they suddenly had motivation to fix it.

author: kazinator
text: Thirty-odd years ago, you could get to a Unix shell from user terminal session of the Vancouver Public Library (British Columbia, Canada) by entering a super long line. From there, even though you were not root, perms on important stuff were wide open: rxwrwxrwx.

It's amazing how similar this exploit payload is to the 20+ year-old Quake 3 vulnerabilities found by Luigi Auriemma (aluigi), which also used the exact same 256-to-1024 character range and nothing more than a long string of AAAA.... Here you're feeding >256 A 's up to a 1024-byte limit to trip musl's defensive length cap, whereas back in the mid-2000s, Luigi was famous for publishing one-line .cfg scripts where the entire exploit was literally "say aaaaa..." repeated a few hundred times overflowing server's memory.¹ ² A great example is Jedi Academy, a 2003 Quake 3 engine game whose multiplayer is still actively played today (its open-source engine port, openjk, is even in the Debian repos btw). Luigi had two classic scripts for it on his site: Jedi Academy <= 1.011 in-game server buffer-overflow ( jamsgbof )¹, which crashed the server just by pushing a string of as past the 1024-byte console buffer, and Quake 3 engine in-game players kicking ( q3msgboom )², where a wall of as hit the engine's 1022-char truncation limit and the leftover bytes confused the parser into disconnecting everyone on the server. Kind of wild that 20 years later, the exact same payload goes from crashing Quake 3 matches from the tilde console to getting root on some SSH servers. [1] https://web.archive.org/web/20101227181948/http://aluigi.alt... [2] https://web.archive.org/web/20060522175643/http://aluigi.alt...

author: thefourthchime
text: It used to be more interesting and elaborate, switching between different models. I used to use Cursor, then Codex, but since Opus 5.5 came out, I just use the Claude IDE. author: cpcdoy
text: I have Claude Ultra, Codex Pro, Cursor, Gemini and Mistral subs. Currently at ~1B tokens/day. I started with Claude Code and Codex in terminal like most people. So I've thought about what my ideal way to ship work was and it goes like this: create a ticket -> an agent makes an interactive plan I can annotate -> implem runs in its own branch/worktree -> checks/diff from the plan make sure the agent writes decent code -> merge. In the end, I simply make sure that I described exactly my expected output and the agents will take care of the matching that. I work on many projects at the same time, maybe there's some kind of ADHD going on, but I usually concurrently manage 10-100 agents at a time while I'm on the go, which means I need a top notch approach to organizing my work (with full capabilities from mobile as well). author: bloppe
text: I recently got really weird with my personal computer after discovering browser DevTools MCP. I basically inverted the relationship between browser and desktop environment, booting directly to a browser in kiosk mode (with Ghostty quick terminal as well, so I always have easy terminal access) and running a local Weston server that shows up as a bookmarked web page on localhost, streamed over vnc, so I can still use legacy gui apps pretty normally if I need to, but I've basically refocused my whole gui environment on the web. I run code-server on localhost instead of VSCode and prefer web apps (often running locally) over traditional GUIs in general. I still use the terminal very heavily as well, and that's where I manage my pi agents. Why? Because the web is an incredibly rich, open, text-based platform with massive representation in training sets, and with tools like DevTools MCP, your agent can do almost anything with your browser: run JS in the page, use the debugger, see network activity; it's extremely powerful. My co-worker does something similar with emacs, another incredibly rich text-based "operating system" like a browser with comprehensive hookability, which he basically uses instead of a desktop environment.

author: glennfiedler
text: I'm juggling multiple claude ultra subs, multiple codex $500 a month subs, antigravity for argon, plus API rate deepseek 4.1 flash, mercury 3, and abliterated large v2 for red teaming. I work across multiple models and harnesses using a really simple redis-backed message bus called "nova-bus": https://github.com/mas-bandwidth/nova-tools (open source). With just this message bus, I can coordinate AIs to work together at a normal pace (worktrees, subtasks etc...), but past a certain point the AIs can't keep up and I need to use a sprint card system I developed to coordinate work. With this sprint system I'm able to work 200 cards wide (each card is around 30-60 minutes of LLM work in a session) across a fleet of 20 machines linked together with tailscale and ssh. Full system is here: https://github.com/mas-bandwidth/nova-sprint (open source) It's been very effective at getting high throughput, but afterwards I find that the resulting code can be a bit of a pastiche from different models working in isolation, thus a good pass over working directly with models to clean up and harden the code is necessary. I find that using nova-bus to coordinate multiple model/harness review of codebase in very effective at increasing code quality. Each model sees things the others don't.

author: FrameworkFred

author: dgunay
text: I use AI primarily through work, I don't pay for a personal AI sub. I do have some OpenRouter credits but I mostly use them sparingly to try open weight models out for small personal projects. I currently interact primarily with Claude Code, but most of my async workers are on Codex. The orchestration part is custom. I talk to a "chief of staff" Opus instance to ingest various workstreams (Jira tickets, alerts, personal ideas, etc) and turn them into beads. It launches workers to tackle individual beads using Remuda, an agent launcher I wrote at work in 2025 and open sourced earlier this year: https://github.com/yendo-eng/remuda . I configure profiles in Remuda that launch containerized agents using my preferred harness and model. I update these profiles as the pareto frontier shifts. Currently it's GPT 6 Luna max for most tasks. It monitors the workers and has them go through at least one round of agentic code review. It surfaces PRs for me to read once they've passed agent review. It then either ships them or hands them off to my coworkers for codebases where I'm not allowed to just merge PRs. Around this workflow I had it write a small collection of skills and scripts to grease the wheels and make repetitive actions more reliable. Since Remuda supports several terminal multiplexers, I've swapped out the backend 3 times: tmux -> herdr-tui -> herdr-core. There's experimental support for Rex but I'm waiting for it to mature a bit before I try and daily drive it. It's not nearly as polished as some of the software factory setups and fancy GUI orchestrators I'm seeing, but it's light, hackable, and so far the bitter lesson has kept this working really well for me so I haven't felt much of a need to try anything else. I have been trying out Muse for a while but it hasn't found a solid place in my life yet. Still too unreliable and too many privacy concerns to justify giving it a lot of access.

author: varenc
text:
Many people report seeing this behavior when using the SEC API specifically which makes me think that service is requesting this.  Maybe email is required by the SEC API? --- UPDATE: The SEC API documentation requires your email in the User-Agent and will reject you otherwise. Demo: U='https://data.sec.gov/api/xbrl/companyconcept/CIK0000320193/us-gaap/Assets.json'
    curl -s -o /dev/null -w 'response: %{http_code}  curl default User-Agent, rejected\n'  "$U"
    curl -s -o /dev/null -w 'response: %{http_code}  email in user-agent, success\n' -A 'Acme Research admin@acme-research.example' "$U"

    response: 403  curl default, rejected
    response: 200  email in user-agent, success SEC docs: https://www.sec.gov/search-filings/edgar-search-assistance/a... So basically Claude is trying to problem solve, and just does what the SEC asks. It's a 'prompt injection attack', but the entity instructing this behavior is the SEC. Tricky alignment problem. Pretty silly mechanism, since of course there's no email validation.  (edit: turns out the SEC will accept most any non-cURL user-agent, email not actually required)

author: grey-area
text: Biggest questions here, which I think need answering: Should Claude have access to user details? I’d say no, unless explicitly entered manually into a chat. Should Claude have access to anything outside of the sandboxed project files without explicit permission? I’d again say no. Should Claude have internet access without a clear log of all requests made? Instances of Claude should be heavily sandboxed and kept away from user data, far more so than they are now. The impression given by the desktop UI is that the LLM only has access to things explicitly added to a project. This impression is not true, as evidenced by Claude pulling data from other sessions outside a project even when not instructed to (I’ve seen this a few times), and in this case pulling your email (from account details, user contacts? I wonder where it got that info?). None of this information should be available to Claude, by design, not by instruction. Using text instructions to try to limit these machines is an incredibly flawed approach and should not be necessary for important info. Anthropic should have the model access completely locked down by controls at the os level over file access, not open by default. That is how to fix this. If a user wants to open access that should be an explicit choice from them, with a warning about possible consequences.

text: I work on Claude Code. We're removing the account email address from the context Claude Code gives the model. Users had reported Claude would hallucinate names for things like @author tags, since it didn't have context on the account. So we added the account email in the model's context for signed-in users. But when Claude wrote a command itself, like a curl call, it sometimes put your email address in the User-Agent as a contact address. Some sites ask agents for a contact, and Claude would sometimes provide the email address in its context. Until the next release arrives, 2.1.317 and later have a built-in mod (on by default) that asks you before Claude runs a web tool call or a curl-style command containing your email (mpoteat covered it here: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50386031 ). But it still doesn't prevent all cases, like when Claude writes a script and runs on its own. The stable channel is still on 2.1.311, so update to 2.1.317 or later. Add the post-pandemic shift to hybrid work and you also see a huge increase of office space vacancies. There's also the fact that property developers, commercial landlords, and institutional lenders frequently favor corporate tenants over independent operators. Rising property values and high commercial rents also price out local, independent owners. However, there have been some exceptions under the New Urbanism banner where you see localized revivals. Some cities (like Jersey City) cap chain occupancy of retail space to 30%. Portland and Austin use zoning rules to make commercial real estate unattractive to chains. Commercial community land trusts can also be used to freeze rent and make space more affordable for local businesses. I doubt there's a one-size-fits-all approach.

author: jimmytehbanana
text: Advertising is a numbers game. The goal isn’t to figure out what you want, it’s to make money. Ads are auctioned off in milliseconds to advertisers betting on what you’re likely to buy. They might know you bought something, but that information isn’t always available. They do know you looked at it though. Historically, people who look at something are more likely to buy it. Maybe you’re still shopping, changed your mind, or need another one. Doesn’t really matter as long as the numbers work out. The UX stuff is pretty obvious. Probably comes down to the time and money involved in implementing and maintaining something better. An engineering problem. The airline stuff is likely an architecture problem. Airlines are notorious for running ancient systems (Windows XP, floppy disks). I’d bet the information is there somewhere, just scattered across a bunch of poorly integrated systems. Like it or not, AI will probably improve a lot of this. As behavioral analysis and AI-generated customer profiles become more common, these systems will get better at figuring out what you actually want. I wouldn’t be surprised to see advertisers running small models built around individual customers and their behavior. You’ll basically just be a vector in some advertising model. The ads will probably be more relevant, but I’m not sure we’ll be thrilled about how much they know about us.

author: autoexec
text: > I have no doubts that a lot of information is being tracked, stored, and sold. Since that's already done, could you guys at least use some of it?.. You can be certain that they are using that data. The truth is that the data being collected about you is not intended to benefit you, it's being gathered and stored and sold to be used against you in any way that the person with that data feels might be an advantage for them. It's not really about showing you relevant ads, or helpful recommendations, or useful product offerings. It hasn't been about any of those things for a very long time now. Your data will still be used that way, but while companies will tell you that is mainly why they collect your data that is a lie. Those are secondary uses for your data and making those things work well for your benefit is a cost to the companies and they are only willing to invest so much time/money/effort into that. Your data is being used mostly for their benefit at your expense, and where it isn't being used today, it's being stored for a time in the future when it can be used more effectively against you. AI promises to make it easier than ever to trawl through all that data and find ways to leverage it to better manipulate you, or take more of your money from you, or further limit any possible risk you might expose a company to. Companies don't want you to be aware of when and how that data is being used, so it's natural for you to feel like it's all being ignored, but you can sure that a lot of work is going into finding new and creative ways to put all that data to use.

The second is the requirement to install a browser extension in order to search from the unified search/url bar. I really wish browser vendors -- or, well, Apple is the only one I care about -- would support it directly. I think they don't want to support a search engine that requires an account. It would be cool if the 100 free searches is progress in this direction but I'm not sure if it will be.

text: I do think it's good that you can now try it out without logging in, but using Cloudflare with aggressive fingerprinting does go a bit against the whole idea of data protection. I'm a Kagi user myself and enjoy using the add-on to take advantage of Privacy Passes. But now I have to assume that I'm still being tracked and that my searches are being linked to me.

author: ActionHank
text: I tried Kagi for a couple of months and then cancelled. I really liked the AI search, but it burns through credits too quickly. I have since switched to using Hermes, it's not quite as good yet, but it's a fraction of the cost. I liked the idea of ad free, slop free search. There were some problems with that though, which were hard to push past. I really like being able to search for stores and local restaurants. Maps integrations were hit or miss, mostly miss. It was also weirdly slow for me, even to load the search page without a query. Final point was their published and then unpublished support of Yandex. The CEO tried to argue some "search without borders" BS, but really they are taking your money that and sending some of it to a Russian company which is either directly or indirectly funding a pointless war. I took issue with that and remembered it every single time I opened the page. In particular it really didn't sit well with me that the response was flippant and then they took down their list of sources. I've switched to DDG and have been happier, YMMV.
